Between the turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, and countless other sides, there’s a lot to keep track of. Thankfully, Panera is stepping in to make sure you can cross at least one thing off your shopping list.

The bakery-café chain is giving away free baguettes on Wednesday, November 25, just in time for Thanksgiving dinner. And considering how expensive holiday grocery shopping can get, I’ll happily take a little free bread.

The giveaway is pretty straightforward: Starting at 11 a.m., customers can visit select participating Panera locations and receive a free baguette with any in-café purchase. That means you can stop by for your usual soup, sandwich, or coffee and leave with an extra loaf of bread for your Thanksgiving table.

Of course, there is one important catch: You’ll need to make a purchase to qualify, so the baguette isn’t entirely free with no strings attached. Plus, each participating café will have only 60 free baguettes on hand, limited to one per person, so you’ll need to act fast if you want to get your hands on one. You can check whether your local Panera is participating on Panera's website or app, or by contacting your local café.

The giveaway is part of Panera’s effort to bring its bread-making tradition to Thanksgiving celebrations nationwide. And while the holiday might be better known for dinner rolls and biscuits, I certainly wouldn’t complain about adding a baguette to the spread.

Having an extra loaf of bread around on Thanksgiving is never a bad idea. Between soaking up leftover gravy, serving alongside dinner, and making sandwiches with whatever turkey survives the night, there are plenty of ways to put it to good use.

And with the giveaway happening the day before Thanksgiving, the timing couldn’t be more convenient for anyone finishing up their last-minute holiday preparations.

#6652. Mario Sorrenti: The Life Behind the Images

During Paris Photo, I visited Mario Sorrenti Diaries, 1991–2000, an exhibition curated by Aaron Stern at LSD, a small gallery on Rue de la Folie Méricourt, in a space that once housed a photographic laboratory. The room was packed, almost overwhelmingly so, and what struck me immediately was the number of young people there. A generation that has grown up with smartphones, accustomed to producing and consuming images at an unprecedented speed, seemed completely fascinated by these handmade books, filled with photographs, Polaroids, contact sheets, handwritten notes, drawings and fragments of a life lived more than thirty years ago.

I found myself wondering what drew them so strongly to these objects. Was it nostalgia for a time they had never experienced? A fascination with the physicality of photography, with the idea that images once existed as tangible things, objects to be touched, collected, cut, pasted and preserved? Or perhaps something more profound: a longing for authenticity, for the traces of real experiences, for a relationship with images that feels increasingly distant from the way we encounter them today?

The more I looked at Mario's diaries, the more I felt that the answer lay somewhere in that last possibility.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

Mario Sorrenti is one of the defining photographers of his generation, an artist whose work has profoundly influenced the visual language of fashion photography since the early 1990s. His contribution to Vogue Italia alone is extraordinary. Over the years, he has created an extensive body of editorials that remain part of the magazine's visual history, images that helped shape not only the aesthetics of fashion but also the way fashion could communicate desire, intimacy and emotion.

His signature is unmistakable, yet it cannot be reduced to a particular technique or aesthetic formula. There is the extraordinary sensitivity with which he approaches light, whether soft and natural or dramatic and carefully controlled. There is his attention to skin, texture and the physical presence of the body, his ability to move between the immediacy of a seemingly spontaneous photograph and the formal sophistication of an elaborately constructed image.

Above all, there is his particular way of representing sensuality.

Fashion photography has always had a complex relationship with desire, and Mario certainly wasn't the first photographer to explore intimacy or eroticism. But he brought something distinctly his own to that tradition. In his photographs, sensuality never feels imposed on the subject. It seems to emerge from the relationship between the photographer and the person in front of his camera. Even when an image is provocative, there is often a tenderness, a vulnerability, an emotional proximity that prevents it from becoming merely an exercise in seduction.

Perhaps the most famous example remains his photographs of Kate Moss, who was his girlfriend at the time, particularly the images that led to the iconic Calvin Klein Obsession campaign in 1993. Their extraordinary power came not simply from Kate's beauty or Mario's photographic talent, but from the genuine intimacy of their relationship. These were not images in which intimacy was staged for the camera. They emerged from an existing emotional connection, from a shared life, before becoming part of the collective visual memory of an era.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

And this is where the exhibition in Paris becomes especially revealing.Rather than presenting the celebrated photographs that established Mario's reputation, it turns its attention to the world from which those images emerged.

The five diaries, spanning the years between 1991 and 2000, bring together photographs, contact sheets, handwritten notes, drawings and fragments of everyday life. For the exhibition, Mario reproduced the pages of his original journals using color Xerox machines, then reassembled and bound them by hand. These are not conventional photographic books, nor simply archival documents. They occupy a fascinating territory between memory, artistic experimentation and the physical act of making.

There are portraits, faces, bodies, moments of everyday life, images of friends and lovers, familiar figures from the fashion world, and deeply personal traces of the people who surrounded him. There are handwritten words, repetitions, experiments, sequences of images that seem to follow the associative logic of memory rather than the conventions of photographic editing.

What makes this particularly fascinating is that Mario's diaries were not simply something he created alongside his photographic career. They were fundamental to its development. He began taking pictures in New York in the late 1980s, teaching himself photography while documenting the world around him, even building a darkroom in his mother's laundry room. It was precisely these personal diaries that, when he showed them to Calvin Klein in 1993, inspired the iconic Obsession campaign.

The boundary between personal work and commissioned photography was never as clear as we might imagine. For many great photographers, this distinction becomes almost meaningless. It is precisely their personal vision, shaped by experiences, relationships and an ongoing process of exploration, that makes their work immediately recognizable, regardless of the context in which it is created. At its highest level, fashion photography is no longer simply in the service of a product, but becomes a space for genuine artistic exploration.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

The photographs are inseparable from the people Mario loved, the places he inhabited and the cultural atmosphere that shaped him. What emerges is not only the development of a photographic language but the formation of a sensibility.

I was particularly touched by this because I lived in New York during those same years. Mario and I belong to the same generation, and although our experiences were our own, we inhabited the same city, at the same moment, within a cultural world that was undergoing an extraordinary transformation.

New York in the 1990s was a place of intense creative exchange, where fashion, photography, music, art and nightlife constantly intersected. There was a sense of freedom, experimentation and possibility, but also a rawness, an urgency, a willingness to take risks and to blur the boundaries between one's personal life and creative work.

Looking through Mario's diaries, I recognized something of that world. Not necessarily the same people or the same experiences, but the atmosphere, the energy, the particular feeling of being young in a city where life and creativity seemed impossible to separate.

There is also the extraordinary family Mario comes from, a remarkable constellation of creative talent. His mother, Francesca Sorrenti, a woman of exceptional talent and an enormously influential figure in the worlds of fashion and image-making; his sister Vanina, an extraordinarily gifted photographer in her own right; and his younger brother Davide, who died tragically young in 1997, an exceptional photographer whose work captured the spirit of a generation with rare sensitivity and immediacy.

In this family, photography has never been simply a profession. It has been a shared language, a way of relating to one another and to the world. Perhaps this helps explain why Mario's work feels so deeply personal, even when it is created within the highly sophisticated machinery of the fashion industry.

Davide's presence in the diaries is particularly poignant. Knowing his story, these images become more than fragments of a shared youth. They are traces of a relationship, of love, of loss, of a world that no longer exists except through the images that remain.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

And this brings us back to something fundamental about photography: its extraordinary relationship with time.

A photograph preserves a moment while simultaneously reminding us that the moment is gone. But in Mario's diaries, this relationship becomes even more complex. Photographs are placed alongside words, drawings, other photographs, fragments of thought. They are revisited, rearranged, reproduced and transformed. Memory becomes an active creative process rather than a passive act of preservation.

The use of Xerox is especially interesting in this respect. Reproduction here is not simply a means of copying an original. It becomes part of the artistic language itself. The texture, the imperfections, the altered colors, the materiality of the pages all contribute to the emotional experience of the work. The diaries remind us that photographs have a physical existence, and that the way we handle, sequence and preserve them can be as meaningful as the images themselves.

In an era when billions of photographs circulate through our screens, when images are increasingly detached from physical objects and, with artificial intelligence, can even be generated without any corresponding lived experience, this feels particularly significant.

We photograph everything, store everything, share everything. Yet how often do we return to those images and give them the attention necessary to become part of our memory? Mario's diaries speak instead of time spent looking, selecting, arranging, touching and remembering: the physical labor of creating meaning from the fragments of one's existence.

And perhaps this is why that small gallery in Paris was so crowded with young people.

I don't think their fascination was simply nostalgic. Nostalgia implies a desire to return to something we have lost, but many of those visitors had never known the world these diaries describe. Perhaps what they were responding to was something more immediate and universal: the evidence of a real life, with all its beauty, contradictions, intimacy and imperfections.

We often discuss the signature of a photographer in terms of light, composition, color or technique. But perhaps the most distinctive element of an artist's visual language lies somewhere deeper, in the particular way they have experienced the world. Before an image becomes iconic, before it enters the history of photography or the collective imagination, it begins with someone looking at something, or someone, and feeling compelled to remember.

Mario Sorrenti Diaries, 1991–2000, curated by Aaron Stern, is on view at LSD, 20 Rue de la Folie Méricourt, Paris, from November 12 to December 10, 2026.

#6651. The Best Frozen Lasagna, According to Our Taste Test

Frozen lasagna is a meal for when you just don’t have it in you. For when you need the comfort of pasta, cheese, and sauce, but you’re not prepared to spend hours boiling, sautéing, and layering. And that’s okay. A great frozen lasagna might not hold a candle to BA’s Best Lasagna, but at the very least it should hold together, with distinct layers, plenty of sauce, gooey cheese, and bouncy pasta.

For this taste test, we sampled nine varieties of store-bought meat lasagna, cooking each from frozen and concealing the brand names from our tasters. Three stood out: Trader Joe’s tasted the closest to homemade, Marie Callender’s was a solid backup, and Rao’s was our favorite for a single serving.

After grumbling our way through several contenders and questioning mankind’s ability to produce a decent supermarket lasagna, Trader Giotto’s Family Style Meat Lasagna restored our faith with a hearty meat sauce and genuinely tasty noodles.

Why it won us over: Trader Joe’s frozen lasagna had a homemade vibe. There were distinct layers of pasta, cheese, and meaty sauce. The cheeses—ricotta, mozzarella, Romano, and Parmesan—each pulled their weight. And the noodles had a fresh bounce. “There’s a whole tomato!” exclaimed senior editor Kelsey Jane Youngman upon finding a chunk of diced tomato in her sample. Other tasters complimented the bright aromatics—fennel was prominent, backed up by oregano and basil. The evenly distributed ground beef and pork were the cherry on top.

Trader Giotto’s Family-Style Meat Lasagna, 32-oz.

More great frozen foods at Trader Joe’s →

Big Lasagna would have you believe you’ll always want to cook a frozen lasagna for a crowd, but sometimes it’s about you and you alone. The 9-oz. Rao’s Made for Home Meat Lasagna is just enough for a single serving—and it doesn’t sacrifice flavor.

Why it won us over: Our tasters were excited to report that Rao’s delivered on structure. While other lasagnas were soupy, floppy, or otherwise unbalanced, Rao’s stayed intact, layer on top of layer, as we ate. It had sturdy (but not tough) noodles, a tomato sauce that was full of umami, and herbal accents that didn’t overpower. Some tasters noted a robust beefy flavor; others were more focused on the garlic and onion. Everyone went in for a second bite.

Maybe you don’t live by a Trader Joe’s—our condolences—and Rao’s proves elusive. You still deserve a serviceable frozen lasagna. Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce offers a sweet and tangy tomato sauce punctuated by well-seasoned meat and noodles that hold their shape.

Why it won us over: This contender avoided many of the pitfalls other brands fell into. It had a solid tomato sauce that was just slightly sweet and tangy, and the meat—both beef and sausage—was flavorful and varied enough in size to give each bite some dynamism. The pasta sheets were springy, not gummy. And while it wasn’t drowning in dairy, there was enough cottage cheese and mozzarella to make itself known.

Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce, 10.5-oz.

We cooked each lasagna from frozen according to its package instructions. While most contenders offered both oven and microwave directions, we stuck with the oven. Tasters sampled each lasagna without knowing which brand they were trying, evaluating each for flavor, texture, and structural integrity. Although Giovanni Rana’s Meat Lasagna is sold refrigerated, we froze it before baking, following the brand’s instructions for cooking from frozen.

The best frozen lasagna should deliver on the fundamentals of structure, flavor, and texture—a tall order for many of our contenders. That meant distinct layers; sheets of pasta that were bouncy, not flimsy; tomato sauce with concentrated flavor and enough body to cling to the pasta; meat that stood out instead of getting lost; and cheese—or many cheeses—that added milky flavor and melty cohesion.

#6649. Thanksgiving Cornbread

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

#6646. How to Survive Politics Talk at Thanksgiving (Without Losing Your Mind)

Thanksgiving is almost upon us, and given that we’re fresh off a midterms blue wave in the US, it’s probably not realistic to expect the holiday to be totally free of political drama. (Unless every member of your family is magically politically aligned on every issue, but when has that ever happened?)

While tapping out of politics talk entirely doesn’t feel like an option in 2026, it feels equally dismal to simply accept a tense or outright hostile environment during what should be a joyful and grateful time of year. Personally, I can vouch for the strategy of finding small political-adjacent moments to unite over, even if they feel frivolous—for example, your DSA-member sister and your establishment-Democrat mom may not align on all of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s policies, but you can probably get them both to agree that watching him personally shovel New Yorkers’ snow last winter was adorable.

For some expert guidance on this issue, Vogue spoke to Dr. Audra Nuru, a professor of communication and family studies at the University of St. Thomas in St. Paul, Minnesota, about how to engage loved ones with differing views in a productive way (and, just as importantly, how to set boundaries when it feels like engagement is no longer good for you and your mental health). Find her thoughts—and some sample scripts she's provided for different conversations—below.

Vogue: How do you recommend preparing for an event or gathering that might include viewpoints you disagree with or find harmful?

Dr. Audra Nuru: It’s true that those kinds of encounters can benefit from a bit of preparation. I like to think of it like packing for a trip to a new and unfamiliar place—you want to be prepared for the expected, but also pack with an open mind for the unexpected. So, before heading into that event, take some time to reflect on what topics might feel a bit sensitive for you, almost like checking the weather forecast, so you can pack accordingly. Remember, everyone is coming to the table with their own unique experiences and perspectives. Embrace those differences with curiosity and kindness. And of course, it’s always wise to set healthy boundaries—that’s like having a good map and a reliable guide to help you navigate any unfamiliar territory.

Is there a subtle, useful way to redirect a political conversation that's starting to feel upsetting?

First and foremost, prioritize the relationship. Remember that the person you’re talking to matters more than proving a point. Ask yourself, “How can I express my views while still showing respect and valuing this person?” Part of showing respect is acknowledging that you may have different perspectives. If a conversation starts to feel a little uncomfortable, try gently saying something like, “I hear you, and I hold a different perspective.” This lets the other person know you’re listening and that their views matter, even if you don’t agree.

Secondly, listen with your heart, not just your head. Truly try to understand where they’re coming from, even if you disagree. What experiences have shaped their beliefs? What emotions are they expressing? And remember, even when it’s tough, try to see things from their perspective. Stepping into another’s shoes, even for a moment, can foster understanding and empathy.

Third, look for points of connection. Even in the midst of disagreement, there’s often some shared experiences or common ground to connect on. It can also be valuable to sense when a conversation needs a pause. If things are starting to feel tense, it’s completely fine to suggest taking a break or shifting to a different topic. Ultimately, navigating difficult conversations with respect is about how we connect, even when we disagree. It’s about building bridges of understanding by making space for different perspectives.

What’s a respectful yet firm way to let someone know their comments have crossed a line?

Using “I” language is such a powerful tool for navigating difficult conversations. Instead of pointing fingers, “I” language lets us shift the focus to our own experience. Imagine saying something like, “I felt uncomfortable when I heard that comment.” It’s honest, it’s respectful, and it avoids making the other person feel attacked. When we own our feelings, it invites the other person to do the same. It creates this space for empathy and understanding, even when we might disagree.

#6643. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

For the Los Angeles premiere of her concert film The JLo Show on Thursday night, Lopez channeled old Hollywood glamour in a Dolce & Gabbana lace gown and an elaborately embroidered opera coat. But it was her jewelry that would really have caught Elizabeth Taylor’s eye: a white-gold Alta Gioielleria Sicilia necklace featuring a whopping 100.10-carat yellow diamond, with matching earrings.

Taylor’s own huge diamond, ruby, and gold archive have been called upon a’plenty: Margot Robbie wore Taylor’s iconic heart-shaped Taj Mahal diamond set in a Cartier necklace while promoting Wuthering Heights, and Kim Kardashian walked the Balenciaga fall 2025 couture show in Paris wearing diamond pendant earrings once worn by Taylor, on loan from jeweler-to-the-stars Lorraine Schwartz. Taylor Swift remains the most ardent modern collector.

Elizabeth Taylor knew a thing or two about a statement jewel. A passionate collector, her jewelry box included a Bvlgari ring featuring a 2.62-carat yellow diamond—a 30th-birthday gift from her fourth husband, Eddie Fisher—and a yellow diamond bracelet gifted to her by Michael Jackson, which fetched £119,700 at auction in 2025. Jennifer Lopez might have a few marriages to go before she catches up with Taylor, but in the jewelry stakes? She’s giving her a run for her money.

#6640. How We Brought a Taste of Maine to Bon Appétit LIVE

Attendees of Bon Appétit Live experienced a taste of Maine through a hands-on lobster cooking class and a demonstration of wild blueberry cornmeal shortcakes, both hosted by Visit Maine.

The class, Lobster 101, was led by Bon Appétit manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Attendees learned how to break down a whole, steamed two-pound Maine lobster and transform the meat into a rich, creamy lobster dip—ideal for holiday hosting. Guests then enjoyed the fruits of their labor, sampling the freshly made dip with Ritz crackers before tasting oysters.

Tripp explained that her oysters, cultivated in the cold tidal waters of the Lower Weskeag River, take three years to reach maturity. Known for their distinctive fluted shells, they offer a briny, mineral-rich flavor balanced by a mellow sweetness.

After years as a lobster harvester, Tripp started Aphrodite Oysters to diversify her lobster business and has since shifted her focus to oyster cultivation full-time. She’s come to appreciate the many environmental benefits of farming and consuming them. Her oysters filter up to 50 gallons of water a day, taking in nitrogen and sequestering some for their growing shells. “Eating an oyster is contributing to the environment,” she declared. Indeed, water test scores have improved at her farm, demonstrating that bivalves help create a healthier ecosystem.

Before the end of the class, a few brave attendees volunteered to shuck their first oysters. Krista guided them through the process, demonstrating how to safely do it at home by protecting the hand holding the shellfish with a towel and gently working the knife into the hinge until the shell released. The well-earned reward was another taste of the Penobscot Bay, as fresh and pristine as the waters themselves.

Later in the day, guests in the Demo Kitchen were treated to Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote, prepared by Bon Appétit senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk. The compote featured wild Maine blueberries from Brodis Blueberries, a multigenerational family farm in Hope, Maine, stewarded by Ron Howard and his family. Howard joined Szewczyk for the demo, where he shared that 99% of the wild blueberries grown and harvested in the United States come from Maine. Attendees learned that they have been growing since the end of the Ice Age, when the tenacious plants, fortified by ericoid mycorrhizal fungi, began to grow and colonize the newly exposed land as glaciers retreated. An important food source for Native Americans, wild blueberries were valued by Indigenous communities for their nutritional benefits well before the modern superfood movement.

Speaking passionately, Howard discussed the many challenges facing Maine growers, including tariffs and currency exchange fluctuations, particularly the impact of a stronger Canadian dollar. Like many Maine farmers, the family has had to get creative. Howard invested in new equipment, including a more efficient type of harvester that allowed the business to scale up and sell to retailers. They created a shelf-stable, freeze-dried product with no added ingredients, allowing them to ship their product beyond the local area. Howard and his son started a distillery, where they use wild blueberries to make an eau de vie and vodka. They have also begun hosting a Wild Blueberry Weekend, opening the doors to the farm and educating the public about the unique benefits of their crop and their growing process.

Carolann Ouellette, director of the Maine Office of Tourism, emphasized that visiting Maine and engaging with local growers and producers such as Howard and Tripp was the best way to experience the state’s diverse bounty. “The relationship between people and nature is inseparable, and stewardship is an important part of the state's identity,” she reflected. Ouellette grew up in New Jersey but relocated to Maine over 40 years ago. Her family used to visit Maine when she was a child, and she recalls those experiences vividly: “As a kid, I remember, when you get to Maine, you can smell the pie or smell the spruce.” It’s those potent memories that drew her to the state permanently, a place she described as “filled with hardworking, welcoming communities that depend on one another.”

A few years ago, Visit Maine began placing greater emphasis on the state’s culinary identity. Ouellette said that awareness of Maine as a food destination continues to grow, “Sea to table with local ingredients is what we were doing before it was a thing.” Beyond the lobster, Visit Maine has been intentional about showcasing the breadth of the state’s agricultural, fishing, and heritage industries. Apples, potatoes, kelp, seaweed, and grains are just a few of the local ingredients featured in Visit Maine’s newsletter and Bountiful Plate video series, which highlights food and beverage producers throughout the state. Ouellette noted that Maine’s food culture is more diverse than many people expect, and its abundance of local products has attracted an interesting mix of exceptional chefs, many of whom are deeply embedded in their communities. Ouellette cited Tripp’s practice of personally delivering her oysters to local restaurants as an example of how the hospitality ecosystem is interconnected.

Most important, Ouellette emphasized that sustainability and stewardship are central to the state’s approach to its food systems and relationship with the landscape. “You can’t get much fresher than food in Maine,” she concluded.

Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Company, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

#6639. BA's Best Orecchiette With Sausage and Broccoli Rabe

Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

#6636. ‘The Body’ Costumes Make for the Ultimate 2000s Period Piece

Costume designer Mirren Gordon-Crozier, who counts the mid-century Lessons in Chemistry and the hyper-contemporary Margo’s Got Money Troubles among her credits, has no trouble flitting between eras. But Netflix’s latest hit, The Body, a coming-of-age psychological drama set at a Catholic high school in 2004, posed a new challenge. “I hadn’t done that period before, even though I lived in it,” Gordon-Crozier tells Vogue. “I was about these girls’s age during that time. I sort of know all these girls, in a way. I think we all do, maybe.”

Gordon-Crozier grew up in London and moved to New York to attend Parsons School of Design, where she adapted to American culture by discerning what signaled status to her classmates. “Having a Balenciaga bag was really important, and that was my main takeaway from college,” she jokes. The City bag does indeed make an appearance, as do a host of other It bags—the Dior Saddle and Louis Vuitton x Takashi Murakami Pochette among them.

“Everything about that era was very important to me because it was also when I was 18 and understanding how you could bond with someone over fashion,” Gordon-Crozier says. Indeed, on-screen interloper Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros) uses fashion to mark her shift from Pentecostal outsider to dance team member. But Gordon-Crozier notes that, although Lisbeth’s sartorial transformation follows her character arc, she ends the season still an outcast. “I think she doesn’t really know about pop culture or any sort of contemporary references at all. I think she was just emulating whatever Anya (Kristina Bogic) was doing,” she says.

A stint at Catholic school also informed Gordon-Crozier’s approach to the costumes. “The way to show your personal style is very minute, since everyone’s skirt has to be the same,” she says. Both on The Body and at her school, girls would roll or alter their skirts to raise the hemline and accessorize their uniforms with designer bags and jewelry. But Gordon-Crozier and creator Quinn Shephard gave themselves an extra challenge. “We set constraints for ourselves: no makeup, no jewelry. Only religious jewelry,” she explains.

One area where there was no room for even subtle individuality? The cutout leotards festooned with teal sequins that the Lions wear as their dance competition costumes. “The girls were not happy about those costumes, let’s just say that,” Gordon-Crozier laughs. “I’m like, You’re not supposed to be happy with them, okay?”

The inspiration came from a surprisingly fashionable source. “I saw this image of Chloë Sevigny in a cutout black bodysuit, probably around the same year,” she says. “It was just with a low-waisted strappy thing—very early 2000s.” Et voilà: with matching dance shoes, thick nude tights in just the wrong shade (Gordon-Crozier notes they are the same brand that Hooters uses for its uniforms), and hair rhinestones, they had the perfect ugly dance costume. “We wanted it to be as tacky as possible, like dance competitions are,” she says.

Offstage, though, Gordon-Crozier assigned each of the girls on the dance team a specific celebrity or pop star to emulate. “Anya always felt like Misha Barton and Sienna Miller, Elise (Sara Boustany) had a lot of Devon Aoki, and then Maddie (Shirley Chen) is Hillary Duff,” she says. “We tried to define every one of them. It just makes it easier when you’re shopping and putting looks together. Everyone has their own color palette, so they’re not really clashing.”

Gordon-Crozier had a particular fondness for Elise’s edgier wardrobe. “Sara personally also has very similar tastes in a way: She likes dark and edgy designers like Comme des Garçons and Plein Sud and Diesel,” she says. It was Boustany’s personal tastes that helped bolster the character of Elise to feel less like a Y2K totem and more like a real person. “I had references for her, but I feel like what we made was more unique. It came alive in the fittings rather than completely copying references.”

#6635. Maple-Sausage Breakfast Casserole

Inspired by the iconic egg and sausage sandwich on a pancake bun, this breakfast casserole is cheesy and just a smidge sweet from the brushing of maple butter at the very end. Destined for holiday brunch tables everywhere and best enjoyed while you’re still in pajamas, this cozy bake will feed a full house. (Don’t be surprised if you find yourself making it again long after the last guest leaves though!)

More high-protein breakfast recipes here.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Lightly coat a 13x9" baking dish with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Whisk 2½ cups (313 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 2 Tbsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Set aside.

Cook 2 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, in a large skillet set over medium-high heat, stirring and breaking into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until browned and cooked through, 10–12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind. Pour fat into a heatproof measuring glass. You want ½ cup fat; spoon out any excess or pour in vegetable oil as needed if you don’t have enough. Stir 2 large eggs and 2 cups whole milk into fat. Let sausage cool slightly, then crumble into small, even pieces with your hands.

Pour fat mixture into reserved dry ingredients and stir until just combined and no large dry pockets of flour remain (batter may be thin and lumpy; it’ll be fine). Set aside ½ cup sausage and ½ cup cheese from 8 oz. sharp yellow cheddar, coarsely grated (about 2 cups), for topping, then add remaining sausage and cheddar to batter and stirring until evenly distributed.

Scrape batter into prepared baking dish and evenly scatter reserved sausage and cheese over. Bake casserole until top springs back when gently pressed with your finger and a tester inserted into the center comes out with just a few moist crumbs attached, 20–30 minutes.

Just before casserole is done, heat 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a small skillet over medium, stirring occasionally, until butter is melted, about 2 minutes.

Brush maple butter over casserole and let cool 10 minutes. Cut into squares. Serve with more maple syrup and butter alongside.

#6633. Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

This baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s important that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

#6631. Sienna Spiro Had Herself a Merry Little Christmas at the Bloomingdale’s x Ralph Lauren Window Unveiling

Having grown up in the U.K., Sienna Spiro never got the chance to soak up the singular type of magic that permeates Manhattan in the lead-up to the holidays. So go figure that at 21 years old, she’d find herself slap bang in the middle of the buzz. On Friday evening, as crowds swarmed Lexington Avenue and 59th Street to catch a glimpse of the breakthrough singer, Spiro was on hand to unveil the Bloomingdale’s holiday windows, created this season in collaboration with Ralph Lauren.

“It’s my first time seeing New York at Christmas. I didn’t even know this [opportunity] was an option. I’m so happy about it,” Spiro told Vogue in the greenroom ahead of the public performance. Even in the context of her “whirlwind” year, it had been quite the week: On Monday, she was announced as a contender for Best New Artist at the 2027 Grammys, and on Wednesday, her name appeared on the lineup for next summer’s Glastonbury festival. “This year has been just insane,” she said. “There’s no fancy word for it. Something new has happened every single day. I can’t really keep up with it to be honest.”

For her latest surreal career moment, the rising star donned a glossy red mackintosh coat from the Ralph Lauren archives, which she paired with black leather driving gloves and sky-high Louboutins—very in keeping with her youthful spin on a vintage-esque look that has been keeping her fans enthralled.

Though she’s not typically swayed by traditional Christmas songs, Spiro thrilled the audience with her one exception: “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas.” “The Frank Sinatra version, of course, with a little saxophone solo,” she noted. Those who had dutifully lined up to hear her smoky tones in real life were delighted when she also launched into “Material Lover” and “Great Expectations.” Indeed, clips of the performance had already made it onto TikTok minutes after she departed the stage—fitting for a performer who was discovered on the platform as a teen.

Just after 7 p.m., Bloomingdale’s CEO Olivier Bron and Ralph Lauren chief branding and innovation officer David Lauren appeared to count down the window and lighting reveal. “We’re bringing two iconic New York brands together, who share the same appreciation for heritage, craftsmanship, and fashion,” Bron said. Behind them, vignettes provided an instant immersion into the plaid- and velvet-drenched world of Ralph Lauren during the holidays.

Post-show, guests, many of whom were dressed in Ralph Lauren, headed back into the department store to see the extent of the festive programming. At Forty Carrots, an UGG takeover sees specialty frozen yogurt on offer, while Roberto Coin has teamed up with Studio 59 on a new Italian menu. Around the store, which felt like an ode to a Love Actually scene, there was everything from a cappella trios and DJs to embroiderers busy at work personalizing presents.

As for Spiro, who had spent the previous night “singing her heart out” when she got to meet her idol Stevie Wonder at Madison Square Garden, she’s doing the holidays a little differently this year, and is set to spend the break in Japan ahead of kickstarting her next tour there in January. “It’s my first time going. I told them I’d play in a Starbucks if I had to, I just really wanted to get there.” With three tours, numerous awards shows, and the festival circuit on the horizon, it’ll be a welcome chance to finally catch her breath.

“I’m really excited to just live a bit, outside of all of this, and grow,” she told Vogue. “I’m still super young. To be a really amazing artist, you’ve got to grow as a person so I’m excited to live, learn, and hopefully end up writing my next record at some point.”

#6629. The Tucson Restaurant Turning Cactus Into Fine Dining

Traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat. Plants armed with burs, barbs, and spines all but scream “do not touch.” For chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee, however, this prickly, dusty landscape stocks a pantry of possibility. The married co-owners of Ursa see the Arizona desert as a rich ground for foraging.

Gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake. Dusty, sage-colored salt bush, when hung to dry, takes on an intensely umami, aquatic saltiness like seaweed. The sweet buds of the Seussian-green palo verde tree become briny, like olives, when suffused with lye.

Don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year. The restaurant processes the young and mature paddles, fruit and their seeds, buds, and flowers, which are then grilled, poached, cold-smoked, juiced, dehydrated, nixtamalized, or preserved into jam, wine, and vinegar.

There are hundreds of edible plants in the Sonoran Desert. Ursa strives to showcase their potential, one 10-course meal at a time.

“We treat Ursa as an art showroom, demonstrating to people what these plants can do, what sustainable means, and what was here before it got easy,” says Lopez. The idea was inspired in part by his Sonoran grandfather, Hector Lopez, who died in the spring. “He was the first person I ever heard say they’re proud to be from the desert,” the chef said.

Ursa began as a pop-up in El Centro, California, in 2023. Lopez and Chee moved to a historic brick building in downtown Tucson, re-opening their doors in October 2025. It’s a homecoming of sorts for the couple, who are both from the Sonoran Desert borderlands. They met in Hawaii, where Chee was working in clean energy and transportation. Lopez, meanwhile, spent roughly 18 years cooking in fine dining and modern progressive restaurants like Redbird and Orsa & Winston in LA, and Pai Honolulu. But he was longing for the desert.

After helping a friend open a restaurant and hosting a few popups in Austin, Lopez and Chee bought a desert foraging guide, packed up their two dogs and began driving around the Southwest. It made sense to settle in Tucson, which was recognized by UNESCO in 2015 as a Creative City of Gastronomy for its continuous 4,000-year agricultural history and deeply rooted Sonoran Desert food traditions.

“That’s a unique thing about being here, the connection from seed to plant to restaurant that we hadn’t been able to grasp before,” Chee says.

Consider a recent course that Ursa built around tepary beans, in which the ancient, nutty bean is refried and topped with h:al squash that’s been lactofermented. The squash’s leaves are fermented to make Japanese-style kosho and its flowers are pickled, dried, crushed with dried saltbush, then tossed with barrel cactus seeds for a desert furikake. It’s served with grilled coins of chorizo made from Lopez’s great-grandmother’s recipe and housemade flour tortillas, to all be washed down with an amazake drink made from fermented wheat and goat fat. Don’t get too attached, however. Riffs owing to finicky ingredient availability occur here almost daily.

Running a restaurant using only ingredients foraged and farmed from within about eight to 10 miles means abiding by pretty intense guardrails. The only wheat used is pima club, an ancient soft white variety cultivated for centuries by the Akimel O’odham (Pima) people. Ursa does not use cucumbers, radishes or citrus.

“We’re not trying to substitute anything, like, ‘How do we achieve cucumber? Let’s grab a cactus,’” Lopez says. “We have to throw everything out, really strip it down. Sometimes we have to let the ingredients be bitter or spicy. We have to put our egos aside and let the ingredient be the star.”

For staff who didn’t grow up or learn to cook here, the learning curve at Ursa can feel a little like alighting on a new planet, even if certain flora happen to resemble prickly weeds in their own backyards.

“We have these really cool moments in the restaurant where people are like, Oh! I have lamb’s quarter just growing in my yard!” Chee says of the spinach-like desert green that appears all over Ursa’s menu.

A young Aaron Lopez with his grandfather Hector Lopez.

Ursa’s approach isn’t always easy for customers to understand, so the couple came up with a more down-to-earth option. This fall, the restaurant debuted a four-course, family-style Lineage menu for $75, alongside the existing 10-course Harvest menu ($150). There’s now a pozole course inspired by the family’s annual springtime tradition of roasting goat in agave leaves, barbacoa-style, and shredding it for soup, and a red masa tamal with glazed quail and yucca blossoms in mole made with burnt mesquite bread, a technique Lopez remembers from childhood.

The idea took shape during Ursa’s extended summer break, as Lopez recovered from foot surgery and reflected on the loss of his late grandfather, the tenacious keeper of family traditions.

“I feel so much closer to my ancestors and the land; we want Ursa to be less esoteric and more soulful,” he says. “The story of Ursa is partly of the desert, partly my family. Now we’ve advanced to the point where they’re symbiotic, and I can't tell them apart.”

#6625. Can a Pre-Nup Be Romantic?

Budgeting, filling out tax forms together, managing family dynamics, and standing in line at city hall: not sexy. Not romantic. Alas, they are the mundane mechanics of even the most thrilling of married lives. Soon after a ring is on the finger, many couples are now discussing prenups—and it’s a topic that brings up unglamorous realities.

No, the administrative process of a prenup isn’t inherently romantic, and let’s not pretend it is. But what it does for the relationship—laying everything bare with radical honesty—is deeply romantic.

“I think navigating something that’s challenging in a relationship and coming out of it aligned is romantic, sexy, and empowering,” says Ashley Hesseltine. The co-host of Girls Gotta Eat spoke openly about choosing to have a prenuptial agreement with her now husband. “But I will not lie. The process of a prenup is inherently annoying, unsexy, and invasive. And it’s admin.”

Wedding planning has a way of sweeping us up into a whirlwind of floral arrangements, seating charts, and linen swatches. Conversations about money, family expectations, and core values naturally come to the forefront next to celebrations.

Luxury wedding planner JoAnn Gregoli agrees that pausing and zooming out to address a prenuptial agreement and the structural foundation of your partnership before you even start picking a venue makes the whole planning process all the more clear. “Marriage isn’t only about romance; it’s also about finances, property, obligations, and decision-making,” she says. “When a couple confronts the subject together, they feel more like they’re entering the marriage as a team and not as a dictatorship.”

You’ve likely already experienced that deep feeling of intimacy with your partner after an exceptionally vulnerable conversation with them. This is just like that. Afterwards, wedding planning transforms from a period of financial tension into one of deep alignment.

It helps, but there’s no requirement to execute a 30-page legal document to reap the emotional rewards of the prenup talk. Some value lies in the vulnerability required to have the conversation at all.

Therapist and author Israa Nasir notes that money remains one of the ultimate taboos in modern relationships, often carrying hidden emotional baggage. “Constructive and supportive conversations can reveal parts of yourself that you otherwise might not—deeper insecurities, past experiences with financial trauma, childhood scarcity, and your relationship with money,” she says. “If your partner doesn’t understand why you behave a certain way about money, it’s harder for them to have empathy for you.”

It may feel like you’re setting up transactional boundaries or betting against your longevity. But in essence, it’s an exercise in radical honesty. Approaching your partner with curiosity rather than judgment is a quick way to turn a wobbly topic fraught with anxiety into a brick in your foundation.

Nobody’s excited about asking their partner about student loans or retirement accounts. It may feel daunting. That’s completely normal.

Start small, and don’t put the pressure on this having to be one big conversation. The first chat can just be about getting their thoughts on prenups in general. Then, you can talk about your thoughts on how you want to manage finances in your relationship. Finally, when you’re ready, you can start diving into assets and what each person wants to walk away with.

The time-old advice of there being no such thing as too much communication stands here. You can even talk about how you want to enter this conversation in a way that might make both of you feel the most comfortable. Agree to enter the discussion with empathy, zero judgment, and positive intent.

Remind yourself that you can frame this discussion around shared goals and mutual care.

Here are a couple of conversation starters:

I’m fairly certain nobody gets married to get divorced. If it does happen, state laws dictate what happens to you both. Letting state statutes dictate your shared destiny? Not romantic. An act of mutual protection? Maybe even chivalrous.

Family and divorce mediator Aswini Puvitharan highlights how modern prenups are moving away from traditional adversarial mindsets. “Prenups are often introduced as ‘How do I protect what’s mine?’ but the better starting point is ‘What would fairness and financial security look like for both of us?’ The more thoughtful prenups today reflect deep care—providing housing, financial support, or protecting someone who takes a career break to raise children.”

Protection from potential bitterness or future legal chaos is inherently loving. “It should feel like you and your partner against the prenup, not you and your partner against each other,” says Hesseltine. “It’s an insurance policy you’re probably never going to use, and if you were strong enough to figure this out together in a healthy way, chances are you’ll never need it.”

#6624. Is Cottage Cheese Good for You?

Yes, cottage cheese is good for you! It's packed with protein and calcium, but the kind you buy matters. Here's how to choose the best cottage cheese for cooking, baking and snacking.

I have to admit: I can see why cottage cheese recipes go viral. TikTok trends have turned this humble dairy staple into everything from high-protein flatbread to better-for-you ice cream. Packed with protein and important vitamins and minerals, cottage cheese is an easy way to make everyday meals more satisfying.

As a dietitian and recipe developer, I love an ingredient that’s not only nutritious but also versatile and affordable, and that can help me meet my daily protein goals. There are so many creative ways to use cottage cheese, and a whole new world of options opens up when you whip it smooth. Think: smoothies, creamy dips, pasta sauces, puddings and more!

But as versatile as cottage cheese is, you can’t swap it into every recipe without a little know-how. And with so many milkfat options, the one you buy matters. I’ll share my favorite ways to use it, which varieties work best for different dishes and a few tricks to help you get delicious results every time.

First things first: Here’s why you might want to toss another tub of cottage cheese into your grocery cart.

Cottage cheese is one of my go-to high-protein foods. A half-cup serving packs 12 to 14 grams of protein, roughly the same amount you’d get from two large eggs.

Adding a scoop of cottage cheese to my plate is an easy way to make meals and snacks more satisfying without turning on the stove. I especially like it at breakfast, when it’s all too easy to end up with a meal that’s heavy on carbohydrates but light on protein. A scoop alongside toast and fruit, or blended into pancake batter, gives breakfast a little extra staying power without much effort.

You don’t have to be lifting heavy weights to care about muscle health. Our bodies need plenty of protein to maintain and repair muscle tissue, and that becomes especially important as we get older.

I like to keep cottage cheese on hand for an easy post-workout snack because there’s nothing to prep. Pair it with fruit or whole-grain crackers, and you’ve got protein plus carbohydrates to help muscles refuel and recover after exercise.

The protein in cottage cheese does more than help keep you full and support your muscles—it also plays an important role in keeping your bones strong. Cottage cheese aprovides two minerals that work together to support bone health: phosphorus and calcium.

It’s worth noting that cottage cheese contains less calcium than a serving of milk or Greek yogurt, but it can absolutely contribute to your daily intake. Just be sure to include other calcium-rich foods in your diet, too.

The type of cottage cheese you buy can make a big difference in how your recipes turn out. Like other dairy products, cottage cheese comes in different milkfat percentages, which affects its taste and texture.

I usually reach for 2% or 4% cottage cheese, depending on how I’m using it. Low-fat (2% cottage cheese) is perfect for whipping into dips, spreads and pasta sauces. It contains enough fat to blend smooth and creamy without feeling too heavy.

Full-fat, or 4% cottage cheese, gets my vote for baked goods, casseroles and lasagna fillings. The extra fat adds richness, which is especially helpful if you’re using it in place of sour cream or cream cheese.

I usually skip fat-free cottage cheese for cooking. It tends to be watery with a slightly chalky taste, and the lack of fat can make creamy recipes less satisfying. That extra moisture can also affect the texture of baked dishes, so I prefer cottage cheese with a little more fat for the best results.

For all its nutritional perks, cottage cheese can also pack a lot of sodium. Some brands contain more than 400 milligrams per half-cup serving. Eat a full cup, and you could be getting more than 800 milligrams of sodium (about one-third of the recommended daily limit) from cottage cheese alone.

Too much sodium can raise blood pressure and increase your risk of heart disease, so it’s worth paying attention to how much you’re getting, especially if you eat cottage cheese regularly.

If you’re watching your sodium intake, compare labels and choose a brand that’s lower in sodium. Good Culture is one of my favorite cottage cheese brands. With 380 milligrams of sodium per serving, it’s a little lower than other brands.

I also go easy on added salt when using cottage cheese with salty ingredients like Parmesan or ranch seasoning.

#6623. Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake

This chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—big, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake layer is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off.

Making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling)

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking).

Whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil.

Do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

Place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

Gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

Beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

Reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

Place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes.

Pour ganache over mousse and smooth with offset spatula. Chill until mousse is completely set (ganache will set in about 30 minutes), at least 4 hours and up to 12 hours (no need to cover unless fridge has other strong smells).

To serve, remove band from base and peel parchment strip away from sides of cake. Transfer cake with base to a plate and let sit 20 minutes; sprinkle top with flaky sea salt.

#6621. How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds. The only ingredients are time and heavy cream. You can use an electric mixer, a whisk, or a mason jar and strong-armed devotion.

In whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop. Desserts like Strawberry Eton Mess or Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake fare best with silky, unsweetened, soft-peaked whip. Others, like this show-stopping Berries and Cream Mille-Feuille, gain structure from sturdier peaks.

To make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk. You can also use a handheld mixer or a mason jar and some elbow grease (more on that later).

If you’re opting for a bowl-and-whisk combo, choose your tools wisely. Cream roughly doubles in volume as you whip it, so use a bowl with three to four times the capacity of your liquid. A large balloon whisk, rather than a narrow sauce whisk, helps incorporate plenty of air into the cream.

Be strategic in the dairy aisle too. Heavy cream and heavy whipping cream contain at least 36% milk fat and can be used interchangeably. Skip anything labeled simply “whipping cream”—or, heaven forbid, “light cream”—which contains less fat and won’t hold its loft as well.

For a basic batch, start with 1 cup cold heavy cream, which makes about 2 cups whipped cream. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, add 1 Tbsp. powdered sugar; for vanilla whipped cream, add ½ tsp. vanilla extract or paste.

With your equipment and ingredients in hand, there are only five steps and infinite possibilities.

Because whipped cream is usually eaten with or as dessert, you might not need to sweeten it at all. To keep flavors balanced, we tend to serve whipped cream au naturel with Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie or Diner-Style Rice Pudding.

But there are no hard-and-fast rules. Maybe you love sweetened whipped cream, or you’re serving it with something less sugary—like, say, a bowl of tart blackberries and torn mint leaves.

For lightly sweetened whipped cream, start with about 1 Tbsp. sugar per cup of cream. Powdered sugar dissolves easily and contains a little stabilizer (usually cornstarch), which can lend the whipped cream some extra holding power. Some cooks prefer the cleaner flavor of granulated sugar, which takes a little longer to dissolve. Either way, add the sugar before you start whipping.

If you’re gazing at a bowl of fluffy, ethereal whip and thinking, “Could I make this even more enchanting?” the answer is yes. There are two primary ways to make flavored whipped cream: infuse or stir.

Kitchen professionals and advance planners tend to cold-infuse. Combine your cream with flavorings like rice (for a creamy Horchata) or bourbon (to take a classic pumpkin pie over the top), then store it in the fridge anywhere from three hours to overnight. Strain out any solids before whipping.

You can also add simple flavorings, like vanilla extract, a small splash of liqueur, cocoa, ground spices, citrus zest, or coffee syrup, before you start whipping. For heavier or chunky additions, such as toasted nuts or chopped chocolate, use a rubber spatula to gently fold them in once the cream is whipped.

Peaks are the shape your whipped cream takes when you pull the whisk out of the bowl and hold it upright like the Statue of Liberty’s torch.

Soft peaks are cloudlike and slump over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks stand upright and hold their shape. Somewhere in between are medium peaks, which have enough structure to hold a shape while remaining soft and supple.

Most Bon Appétit recipes, such as these Mix-and-Match Fools, involve whipping cream to soft peaks. That velvety texture is our go-to when we’re dolloping whipped cream atop pecan pie.

But we aren’t always such softies. Medium peaks help this Ginger-Raspberry Icebox Cake keep its shape. And old-fashioned chocolate mousse involves whipping batches of cream into stiff and soft peaks: The former is folded into the chocolate mixture for structure, while the softer stuff tops the dessert.

By hand: Our preferred method, whipping cream by hand requires the most time and effort, but it also gives you optimal control over its final texture. Even if you use a mixer to get your whipped cream started, switching to a whisk for the final few moments makes it easier to stop exactly where you want.

In a Mason jar: No whisk? No mixer? No problem. To make whipped cream with your bare hands, put a container with a tight-fitting lid, large mason jar, or leak-proof cocktail shaker into the freezer for five minutes. Get the heavy cream very cold and make sure you have ample headspace in your vessel of choice. About one cup of liquid in a four-cup container is a good amount.

Secure the lid and shake it like you mean it. For the creamiest results, a consistently assertive pace is better than intermittent spurts of brute force. When the liquid stops sloshing and starts feeling and sounding heavier, open the lid and take a peek. If it looks underwhipped, close it back up and keep shaking.

Good news for meal preppers: You can make whipped cream hours in advance. Err on the side of underwhipping it during your prep. Store the lightly whipped cream, covered, in the fridge for up to four hours before serving, then give it a few energetic whisks to bring back its bounce right before you dollop it onto dessert.

You can also freeze whipped cream (no, seriously). It takes a bit of effort, though. Line a baking sheet with parchment, then pipe or scoop spoonfuls of whipped cream onto it. Freeze until the whipped cream nuggets are solid, then peel them off the parchment and store them in an airtight bag in the freezer for one to two months. When you’re ready to serve, let them thaw at room temperature for about 15 minutes.

Instant vanilla pudding is the key to luscious, long-lasting whipped cream.

Need it to hold up longer? Instant vanilla pudding mix is one of BA’s favorite shortcuts for stabilized whipped cream. For every cup of heavy cream, add 1 Tbsp. instant vanilla pudding mix (call it pastry cream powder if anyone gives you sass) and 2 tsp. powdered sugar, then whip as usual. The modified starch in the pudding mix absorbs excess moisture and helps prevent the cream from separating, keeping it fluffy for up to 24 hours.

For something tangier, sour cream adds both flavor and body. Our Pecan Cream Pie whisks ¼ cup sour cream into 1 cup heavy cream; the sour cream cuts the richness while helping the topping hold its shape.

In any case, your dinner party guests don’t have to sit quietly as you furiously whisk their dessert topping to order. Prep work never tasted so sweet.

If your whip isn’t coming together quite right, don’t fret. Simple solutions abound.

This is probably a temperature issue. Cold cream whips more readily and holds onto the air you’re incorporating more effectively, so it comes together faster—and stays fluffy longer. Pop the bowl, whisk, and cream back into the freezer for five minutes, or into the fridge for up to 30. Once everything is cold, resume whisking.

Another possible culprit is the fat content of your cream. Opt for heavy whipping cream or heavy cream over half-and-half or other heavy cream substitutes.

If the cream is just a little too stiff or starting to look grainy, add a splash of chilled heavy cream and slowly whisk it in. Add more, a little at a time, until the texture smooths out.

Keep a close eye on it: If you whisk for too long, you’ll end up with a bowl of butter.
